sources.title: ICC Safety module (ISO 45001) page
supportedClaims: The published ICC page describes incident and near-miss reporting in which severity is set from the level of harm. These are published descriptions; availability and configuration must be confirmed in a demonstration and no capability is advertised as verified.
The page describes a QR code on the floor that opens an anonymous report form with no login, and anonymous reports appear in the safety dashboard marked as anonymous.
The page describes a health and safety dashboard with its own permissions, separate from quality, switched on per organization.
The page states incidents that need corrective action are carried into the Improvements module, and the auditor view shows corrective actions linked to each incident.
The page describes an auditor view with the incident and near-miss log showing severity and status, floor reports including anonymous ones, and linked corrective actions.

The page maps the module to ISO 45001:2018 clauses 10.2 (incident, nonconformity and corrective action), 5.4 (consultation and participation of workers) and 6.1.2 (hazard identification and assessment of risks and opportunities); a mapping is not a statement that software alone satisfies a clause.

The page describes setup in four steps: map processes with named owners, configure modules (fields, checklists, terminology, routing), onboard standards, and deploy to the floor with training and a certified consultant reviewing configuration through to audit.
The page states every AI output is a suggestion that a person reviews before it enters a controlled record.
The page describes the problem as near-misses going unreported because reporting needs a form and a supervisor, investigations starting from a blank page, and committees not seeing patterns early.
The page does not state pricing, notifications or alerts, injury classification beyond severity, regulatory or authority reporting, e-signatures or PIN access; those are evaluation questions.

ROOT-BROWSER-VERIFIED on 2026-11-19: Codex root directly read the primary ICC Safety page in Chrome. It describes severity by harm, an anonymous QR no-login form, separate dashboard and permissions, corrective-action handoff, and numbered configuration sections 01–04 for mapping, configuring modules including fields, checklists, terminology and routing, onboarding standards, and deployment and training. These are vendor descriptions, not a verified plant condition or guaranteed implementation workflow. Exact anonymous-form field configuration, selectable severity levels and handoff mechanics remain unconfirmed.

sources.title: Guide for health and safety committees and representatives
sources.publisher: Government of Ontario, Ministry of Labour
supportedClaims: ROOT-BROWSER-VERIFIED: Codex root directly read this primary Ontario government page in Chrome on 2026-11-19. The displayed title is Guide for health and safety committees and representatives and the page showed Updated August 17, 2026. Automated HTTP retrieval remains blocked with 403; no successful automated fetch is claimed.

Ontario thresholds generally use regularly employed workers. Workplaces with 6–19 generally select a representative where no joint health and safety committee is required. Designated-substance rules and director or minister orders can require committees below 20; construction and farming have specific provisions.
At least half of committee members are workers who do not exercise managerial functions.
Joint health and safety committees meet at least every three months. Worker workplace inspections are monthly, subject to the stated inspector, regulatory and impracticability exceptions.
Employers respond to written recommendations within 21 calendar days, providing an implementation timetable for accepted recommendations and written reasons for rejected recommendations.
These are Ontario-specific guide descriptions with qualifications and exceptions; legislation governs.

mapping-workflows.description: Mapping the current process for incident and near-miss reporting software: define the problem, trace reports and handoffs, and assign owners and decisions.

boundaries: Map the existing reporting path and handoffs; leave vendor comparison to the evaluation chapter.
Leave form design, severity rules and corrective action mechanics to their own chapters.

subsections.title: Define the reporting problem
keyPoints: Describe the problem in operating terms: incidents and near-misses reported on paper or by email are not consistently logged, rated for severity or linked to corrective action.

The ICC Safety page describes the same pattern: near-misses go unreported because reporting needs a form and a supervisor, investigations start from a blank page, and committees see patterns late. Present it as the vendor's description of the problem, not as measured data.

workflow.input: Paper forms, emails, whiteboard notes and any existing log
workflow.decision: Decide what counts as an incident, a near-miss and a hazard report in this organization
workflow.exception: A report arrives that fits no definition

evaluationCriteria: Can the team state which events must be logged and who decides in a doubtful case?
subsections.example: A supervisor finds three differently worded notes about the same guard gap in three places.

subsections.title: Trace reports, records and handoffs
keyPoints: Follow one real report from the person who saw the event to closure and note every record, hand-off and delay.
Note where information is retyped, lost or left only in an email thread.

workflow.input: One recent report and every document it produced
workflow.decision: Decide which steps are required and which are habit
workflow.exception: A report stalls because the supervisor is absent

evaluationCriteria: Does the map show every place a report can be lost or delayed?
subsections.example: A map shows that a floor report waits for the supervisor to return from a meeting before anyone logs it.

subsections.title: Assign owners and decisions
keyPoints: Name an owner for intake, severity rating, investigation and corrective action follow-up.
Where a joint health and safety committee or representative exists, Ontario's guide describes its role; check the rules for the relevant province instead of assuming Ontario's apply nationally.

workflow.decision: Assign a named owner and a backup to each decision
workflow.exception: An owner leaves or is unavailable

evaluationCriteria: Can every step name an owner and a backup?
subsections.example: A table shows no owner for rating reports that arrive on night shift.

subsections.title: Set acceptance criteria for the software
keyPoints: Turn the map into measurable acceptance criteria for a demonstration: report filed from the floor, severity recorded, action linked.
Treat each criterion as an evaluation question, because published descriptions are not verified capabilities.

workflow.decision: Decide which steps the software must support first
workflow.exception: A criterion cannot be tested with sample records

evaluationCriteria: Is each criterion testable with a real report and its exceptions?
subsections.example: The list asks a demonstration to show an anonymous floor report becoming a linked action.

mapping-workflows.scope: Cover the current-state map of incident and near-miss reporting, its records, handoffs and owners.

evaluating-software.title: Evaluate incident and near-miss reporting software
evaluating-software.description: Evaluating incident and near-miss reporting software: build a workflow-based shortlist, test decision points, and examine permissions, evidence and support.
evaluating-software.chapterKeyword: incident and near-miss reporting software evaluation
boundaries: Cover vendor evaluation; the current-state map belongs to the mapping chapter.
Leave configuration of forms and severity to later chapters.

subsections.title: Build a workflow-based shortlist
keyPoints: Shortlist by workflow fit, not feature count: floor reporting, severity, investigation, linked corrective action, auditor view.
The ICC Safety page describes incident and near-miss reporting, QR-code anonymous reporting, a separate safety dashboard and linked corrective actions; confirm each in a demonstration.

workflow.decision: Decide which vendors can demonstrate the full path
workflow.exception: A vendor shows features but not the path

evaluationCriteria: Does every shortlisted vendor handle the end-to-end path with your sample reports?
subsections.example: A team drops a vendor that cannot show a report becoming an action.

subsections.title: Test the decision points
keyPoints: Bring real reports, including an anonymous one and a disputed severity rating, and watch each decision being recorded.
The page states severity is set from the level of harm; ask how the scale is configured and who may change a rating.

workflow.decision: Decide whether each decision is captured and attributable
workflow.exception: The demonstration uses clean sample data only

evaluationCriteria: Were exceptions demonstrated, not just the happy path?
subsections.example: A scoring sheet marks a rating change as unrecorded.

subsections.title: Examine evidence, permissions and AI use
keyPoints: The page describes a separate health and safety dashboard with its own permissions, enabled per organization; ask who can see which reports and how anonymous reports are protected.
The page states every AI output is a suggestion a person reviews before it enters a controlled record; ask what AI does in the module.

workflow.exception: Safety data needs to be hidden from quality users or the reverse

evaluationCriteria: Can access be limited by role and reviewed?
subsections.example: A matrix shows investigators need wider access than floor reporters.

subsections.title: Compare setup, cost and support
keyPoints: The page describes four setup steps: map processes, configure modules, onboard standards, deploy to the floor with a certified consultant reviewing configuration through to audit.
Pricing, notifications and regulatory reporting are not stated on the page; request written answers.

workflow.decision: Decide whether setup effort and support fit
workflow.exception: A vendor will not commit answers in writing

evaluationCriteria: Are cost, setup effort and support responsibilities written down?
subsections.example: The team lists unanswered questions beside each vendor.

evaluating-software.scope: Cover a workflow-based evaluation of incident and near-miss reporting software, including what ICC publishes and what remains an evaluation question.

reporting-intake.title: Design reporting intake for incident and near-miss reporting software
reporting-intake.description: Designing intake in incident and near-miss reporting software: define report fields, enable anonymous floor reporting, and make the report easy to start.
reporting-intake.chapterKeyword: incident and near-miss reporting software intake
boundaries: Cover how a report is started and captured; rating and triage belong to the severity chapter.
Leave investigation methods to the investigation chapter.

subsections.title: Define the report fields
keyPoints: Keep the first form short: what happened, where, when, who was affected and whether anyone was hurt.
Separate required fields from those added later by the investigator.
evaluationCriteria: Can a floor reporter finish the form quickly?
subsections.example: A form drops six optional fields after a test.

subsections.title: Support anonymous floor reporting
keyPoints: The ICC page describes a QR code on the floor that opens an anonymous report form with no login, and anonymous reports shown in the dashboard marked as anonymous.
Decide when anonymity is allowed and how follow-up questions are handled when the reporter is unknown.

workflow.decision: Decide whether anonymous reports are accepted and who reads them
workflow.exception: An anonymous report names a person

evaluationCriteria: Does the tool mark anonymous reports and keep them in the same log?
subsections.example: A policy allows anonymous reports and assigns the safety coordinator to read them first.

subsections.title: Make reporting reachable on the floor
keyPoints: Place access points where events happen; test lighting, gloves, connectivity and language.
The page does not mention PIN access or notifications; treat those as questions.
evaluationCriteria: Can a report be filed at the point of work?
subsections.example: A trial shows one dock has no signal and needs a different access point.

subsections.title: Review new reports on arrival
keyPoints: Set a response time for first review and an owner for each shift.
Record that a person reviewed the report, even when no action follows.

workflow.decision: Decide to rate, investigate or close

evaluationCriteria: Is there evidence that each report was reviewed?
subsections.example: Every report in the queue shows a reviewer and a date.

reporting-intake.scope: Cover report fields, anonymous floor reporting, shop-floor access and first review of a new report.

severity-triage.title: Rate severity and triage in incident and near-miss reporting software
severity-triage.description: Severity and triage in incident and near-miss reporting software: set a harm-based scale, rate reports consistently, route them and handle disputed ratings.
severity-triage.chapterKeyword: incident and near-miss reporting software severity
boundaries: Cover rating and routing; the investigation itself belongs to the next chapter.
Avoid legal reporting thresholds; they depend on jurisdiction.

subsections.title: Define a harm-based scale
keyPoints: The ICC page states severity is set from the level of harm; define each level in plain words with examples before configuring anything.
Rate near-misses by potential harm, and say so explicitly.

workflow.exception: A level has no clear boundary

evaluationCriteria: Do two raters give the same rating to the same report?
subsections.example: Two coordinators rate the same report differently and rewrite the definition.

subsections.title: Route reports by rating
keyPoints: Decide who is told about each level and how fast.
The page does not state notifications or alerts; ask how routing and reminders work.
evaluationCriteria: Does a higher rating reach the right person quickly?
subsections.example: A routing table sends the highest level to the plant manager the same shift.

subsections.title: Handle disputed ratings
keyPoints: Allow a rating change with a reason and a name.
Keep the original rating visible.
evaluationCriteria: Is every rating change attributable?
subsections.example: A report is re-rated and the log shows both ratings and the reason.

subsections.title: Separate regulatory duties from the log
keyPoints: Reporting duties to authorities depend on the province and the event; the ICC page does not describe regulatory reporting, so treat it as an open question.
Ontario's guide describes committees and representatives, not reporting deadlines; confirm duties with the relevant authority.

workflow.decision: Decide which events need external notice

evaluationCriteria: Does the team keep its external reporting checklist separate and current?
subsections.example: A checklist lists the authority contact for each province of operation.

severity-triage.imageBrief: A safety coordinator reviewing reports at a dock office desk; authentic manufacturing environment, no readable text or logos
severity-triage.scope: Cover a harm-based severity scale, triage routing, rating disputes and escalation.

investigation.title: Run investigations from a structured record
investigation.description: Running investigations in incident and near-miss reporting software: assign an investigator, gather evidence, find causes and record conclusions.
investigation.chapterKeyword: incident and near-miss reporting software investigation
boundaries: Cover the investigation; corrective action tracking belongs to its own chapter.
Do not specify a single root cause method as required.

subsections.title: Assign and scope the investigation
keyPoints: The ICC page says investigations otherwise start from a blank page; ask how the record carries the original report into the investigation.
Match investigation depth to severity.

workflow.decision: Decide who investigates and how deeply

evaluationCriteria: Does the investigation begin with the original report attached?
subsections.example: A medium report gets a short investigation; a higher one a team.

subsections.title: Collect evidence
keyPoints: List evidence types: statements, photos, equipment records, training records.
Keep evidence with the incident record.
evaluationCriteria: Is evidence retrievable from the incident record?
subsections.example: An investigator links the machine record and the operator's training record.

subsections.title: Analyze causes without blame
keyPoints: Use a method the organization already trains on; the software should record, not dictate.
Look at process and condition causes first.
evaluationCriteria: Does the record separate facts from conclusions?
subsections.example: A cause statement points to a missing guard check, not a person.

subsections.title: Record conclusions and review
keyPoints: Require a reviewer to accept the investigation before closing.
Where AI drafts anything, a person reviews it before it enters the record, as the ICC page states.
evaluationCriteria: Is there a visible review step?
subsections.example: A reviewer returns an investigation lacking evidence.

investigation.imageBrief: An investigator interviewing an operator beside a machine guard; authentic manufacturing environment, no readable text or logos
investigation.scope: Cover investigation assignment, evidence, cause analysis and recording conclusions.

corrective-actions.title: Link incidents to corrective action and follow-up
corrective-actions.description: Linking incident and near-miss reporting software to corrective action: decide which reports need action, assign owners, track due dates and verify results.
corrective-actions.chapterKeyword: incident and near-miss reporting software corrective action
boundaries: Cover action from incidents; general corrective action practice belongs to the CAPA guide.
Leave committee trend review to the committee chapter.

subsections.title: Decide which reports need action
keyPoints: The ICC page says incidents that need corrective action are carried into Improvements; ask what is carried across.
Set criteria: severity, repeat occurrence, open hazard.

workflow.exception: Action not needed but concern remains

evaluationCriteria: Is the reason for no action recorded?
subsections.example: A low-rated repeat event gets an action.

subsections.title: Assign owners and due dates
keyPoints: Name one owner and a date.
Ask whether reminders exist; the page does not state them.
evaluationCriteria: Does every action have an accountable owner?
subsections.example: A maintenance lead accepts a guard fix with a date.

subsections.title: Keep the link to the incident
keyPoints: The page says auditors can see corrective actions linked to each incident.
Check that an incident cannot close while its action is open.
evaluationCriteria: Can one incident show all its actions?
subsections.example: An incident shows two linked actions, one open.

subsections.title: Verify effectiveness
keyPoints: Check after a set period that the hazard is controlled and similar reports have stopped.
Record who checked.
evaluationCriteria: Is effectiveness checked, not only completion?
subsections.example: A check finds a repeat report and reopens the action.

corrective-actions.imageBrief: A supervisor and maintenance technician reviewing a fixed machine guard; authentic manufacturing environment, no readable text or logos
corrective-actions.scope: Cover the decision to act, linking to Improvements, ownership, effectiveness checks and closure.

committee-visibility.title: Give committees and workers visibility into incident data
committee-visibility.description: Using incident and near-miss reporting software with safety committees: share dashboards, review patterns, support worker participation and respect permissions.
committee-visibility.chapterKeyword: incident and near-miss reporting software committee
boundaries: Cover committee and worker visibility; do not restate investigation steps.

subsections.title: Share the right dashboard
keyPoints: The ICC page describes a separate health and safety dashboard with its own permissions; ask what a committee member can see.
Decide whether anonymous reports show to the committee.
evaluationCriteria: Does the committee see what it needs and no more?
subsections.example: Committee members see counts and statuses, not names.

subsections.title: Review patterns on a set rhythm
keyPoints: Ontario's guide describes a joint health and safety committee meeting at least once every three months and a worker member inspecting the workplace at least once a month, for the workplaces it covers.
Use the log to prepare each meeting; the page says committees otherwise see patterns too late.
evaluationCriteria: Does the meeting pack come from the log?
subsections.example: A chair lists three repeat locations for discussion.

subsections.title: Handle committee recommendations
keyPoints: Ontario's guide says an employer must respond in writing within 21 days to written committee recommendations; confirm current requirements.
Track recommendations like actions.
evaluationCriteria: Is each recommendation answered and tracked?
subsections.example: A recommendation is logged with a response date.

subsections.title: Support worker participation
keyPoints: The ICC page maps the module to ISO 45001:2018 clause 5.4, consultation and participation of workers; a mapping is not proof of compliance.
Share outcomes with reporters.
evaluationCriteria: Do reporters see that reports lead to action?
subsections.example: A board shows fixes made from floor reports.

committee-visibility.scope: Cover dashboards, trend review, worker participation, and committee duties as described by Ontario guidance.

Rehearse the audit view with sample records.

keyPoints: The page maps the module to ISO 45001:2018 clauses 10.2, 5.4 and 6.1.2.

keyPoints: Decide which historical records to import; ask how the import works, as the page does not describe it.

mapping-workflows.summary: The page maps the current-state incident and near-miss reporting workflow across four subsections that match the plan exactly. All factual claims about ICC Safety capabilities are correctly framed as published descriptions requiring demonstration confirmation. The Ontario JHSC source is cited only where Ontario-specific regulatory content is discussed, with an explicit caution against assuming those rules apply nationally. Workflow elements (role, input, decision, record, exception) are present in each subsection. Illustrative examples are labeled and use an unnamed Canadian manufacturer. No FAQ section appears, which is correct because the plan assigns none. The changed paragraph correctly presents ICC Safety page content as a vendor problem description rather than measured data. No previous findings were raised. Links use the two supplied source URLs plus an allowed internal path. No scope boundary violations were detected.

A condition someone noticed before any event occurred.

A step in the reporting process after which no record shows a decision was made, leaving a report unresolved.
